sheet: The obligation to examine who bears the costs and receives the benefits of environmental decisions, including distributive, procedural, and recognition justice dimensions.

Indigenous peoples' collective rights to govern decisions affecting their lands, knowledge, and data — including FPIC, data sovereignty (CARE Principles), and self-determined participation. Distinct from L1: a project can distribute benefits equitably while still violating governance rights.
The obligation to make decisions, analyses, and their basis visible, and to ensure that someone bears consequence for decisions affecting others.

The ethics of deliberate ecological manipulation — whether intervention is justified, at what scale, with whose authorization, and with what obligations regarding reversibility and precaution. Triggers when management action creates conditions without historical precedent or is practically irreversible.

Obligations practitioners carry when institutional pressures conflict with duties to the public and to ecological systems — including honest reporting, conflict-of-interest disclosure, and the conditions under which professional deference to organizational authority is or is not appropriate.

field: Skill Area 7.1 (Professional Ethics Architecture) uses E/A only — no Implicit values. These competencies were designed to make ethical content constitutive, so the E/A binary applies a constitutive test: E means removing the lens would collapse the competency's argument. Skill Area 7.2 (Human-AI Professional Practice) uses the standard E/I/A vocabulary.

Across the taxonomy, approximately 95% of ethical content is implicit rather than explicit. This ratio is itself a significant finding — it indicates that existing professional competency standards embed ethical obligations in practice without providing practitioners shared vocabulary for recognizing or reasoning about them. Intervention Ethics (L4) has zero explicit treatments in Domains 1–6 despite governing high-consequence ecological decisions.
